In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence for the role of antioxidants in preventing the development of CVD is still insufficient and that the results from the studies are inconsistent.
there is no evidence to support the use of vitamin C in the treatment of any condition in the absence of a specific deficiency.
the use of vitamin C in the treatment of chronic kidney disease is not recommended.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of vitamin E and vitamin C in combination is beneficial for the prevention of CVD, but not when used alone.
the oxidation of LDL in ESRD patients is not only due to the presence of the uremic milieu but also to the low levels of antioxidants.

we found that vitamin C is an essential cofactor for the activity of several enzymes involved in the metabolism of amino acids and other nutrients, and that the lack of this vitamin in the diet of rats results in a reduction of the activity of these enzymes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the 2-DE proteomic approach is a valuable tool to study the molecular mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of renal disease.
the oxidation of lipoproteins is a very complex and multi-step process, and the role of vitamin C in this process is still not fully understood.

the use of the vitamin C and E supplements in the diet of the patients with chronic renal disease may be a useful tool for the prevention of the development and progress of renal disease and for the prevention of cardiovascular complications in these patients.
